questions.q: In this lab's worked scenario, how is a single gate's combined error probability computed from its decoherence and depolarizing probabilities?
options: combined_error = decoherence_prob + depolarizing_prob − (decoherence_prob × depolarizing_prob), treating the two sources as independent events
combined_error = decoherence_prob × depolarizing_prob only, ignoring either probability alone
combined_error = decoherence_prob − depolarizing_prob, since the two sources cancel each other out
combined_error is always equal to whichever of the two probabilities is larger, with the smaller one ignored entirely
questions.explain: The lab treats the two error sources as independent events, so P(error on this gate) = decoherence_prob + depolarizing_prob − (decoherence_prob × depolarizing_prob), equivalent to 1 minus the product of each source's survival probability.

questions.q: In the lab's worked example, what is Gate 3's (200 ns) combined per-gate error probability?
options: Approximately 1.9980 × 10⁻³ (the decoherence probability alone, with no depolarizing contribution)
Exactly 0.001 (the depolarizing probability alone, with no decoherence contribution)
Approximately 2.9960 × 10⁻³
Approximately 5.6853 × 10⁻³ (the full three-gate circuit total)
questions.explain: Gate 3 combines its decoherence probability (≈1.9980×10⁻³) with its depolarizing probability (1.0×10⁻³) to get a combined error of ≈2.9960×10⁻³ -- the lesson notes this is close to the simple sum because the correction term (their product) is negligible at this scale.

questions.q: How is the overall probability that the full three-gate circuit survives cleanly computed from the three individual per-gate survival probabilities?
options: By adding the three per-gate survival probabilities together
By averaging the three per-gate survival probabilities
By taking only the smallest of the three per-gate survival probabilities and discarding the other two
By multiplying all three per-gate survival probabilities together (0.998800 × 0.998501 × 0.997004 ≈ 0.994315), since the circuit only survives cleanly if every gate individually survives
questions.explain: Independent-event composition means the probability all three gates succeed is the product of their individual survival probabilities: 0.998800 × 0.998501 × 0.997004 ≈ 0.994315, giving a total error probability of about 1 − 0.994315 ≈ 5.6853×10⁻³.

questions.q: What is the lab's final computed total error probability across all three sequential gates, and roughly what does it mean?
options: Approximately 5.6853 × 10⁻³, meaning roughly a 0.57% chance (worse than 1-in-200) that at least one error occurred somewhere in just this small three-gate circuit
Exactly 100%, meaning an error is guaranteed on every single run of the circuit
Approximately 1.9980 × 10⁻³, equal to just the largest single gate's decoherence probability
Approximately 0.057%, meaning errors are essentially negligible at any circuit depth
questions.explain: 1 − 0.994315 ≈ 5.6853×10⁻³, or about 0.57% -- worse than 1-in-200 odds of at least one error across only three gates, which is the number the lesson uses to motivate how quickly error probability compounds as circuits get deeper.

questions.q: Why does the lesson stress that every number in this lab is explicitly illustrative rather than a measurement from a real processor?
options: Because the chosen T1, depolarizing rate, and independent-event composition model are simplifications -- real circuits also involve correlated errors, leakage, and readout errors not captured by this simple model, so the value of the exercise is the method, not the exact digits
Because illustrative numbers are always exactly 10x larger than real hardware numbers
Because the numbers are deliberately wrong and should not be trusted for any purpose
Because real quantum hardware has no measurable error rates at all
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this is a simplified, illustrative model -- real circuits have additional complications like correlated errors and readout errors not modeled here -- so the lab's point is to teach the composition method, not to assert these are measured hardware specs.
